extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, and law students/practitioners dealing with U.S. patent interference practice
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules governing interference proceedings in U.S. patent practice: grounds for dissolution or suspension, amendment/disclaimer practice, jurisdictional limits of interference examiners, appeals, and the legal effect of interference judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for motion to dissolve an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The grounds on which a motion to dissolve may be based are the non-patentability of the invention, the absence of any real conflict between the claims of the several contestants, the failure of either party to show that he is a true inventor of the invention claimed, or such irregularity in the institution of the interference as must render any judgment therein void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion may be based on non-patentability, lack of actual conflict, lack of inventorship, or procedural irregularity. From the decision of the primary examiner upon this motion an appeal lies to the examiners‑in‑chief; if no appeal taken within prescribed time, other remedies exist (e.g., appeal to Commissioner, bill in equity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions based on patentability must be sent to the primary examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: If a motion to dissolve an interference is based on want of patentability, it must be sent to the primary examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An interference examiner cannot decide questions of patentability; such motions are remitted to the primary examiner (see Green v. Hall). If the primary examiner overrules and affirms prior findings, mover may protest to the Commissioner; appeal lies to examiners‑in‑chief. If suspension/remand occurs, interference may be dissolved pro hac vice and the applications treated ex parte until resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to dissolve may be filed at any time (subject to timing rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve a motion may be made at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a motion can be made at any stage, certain timing constraints apply: if not filed within twenty days after the statement is approved, delay must be explained or the examiner of interferences will not send the case to the primary examiner (appeal to Commissioner remains possible). Some motions (e.g., non-patentability) should be made at the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents required in a motion to dissolve
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve an interference must state the reasons, cite the grounds, and show all the facts on which the motion is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions should present all factual allegations and legal grounds. Irregular or insufficient motions will be dismissed. The tribunal will consider only the motion and the papers filed (counter‑affidavits may be permitted under rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service and notice for motions in interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverse parties must be served with a notice of a motion to dissolve an interference and with the reasons therefor, and have an opportunity to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice to all parties is required because an interference is a contested case even at preliminary stages; failure to give notice may render motion irregular. On receipt of notice, time limits for appeal/run start (e.g., ten days from receipt in some contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular motions will be dismissed
rubrics_metrics.description: An irregular motion to dissolve an interference will be dismissed on motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions not complying with required form, timing, or substance (e.g., relying on outside matters not in the application) are subject to dismissal (see cited cases). Parties should ensure motions are properly grounded and presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions based on matters outside the application (preliminary statements) are improper
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve an interference must be based on the application alone, not on the preliminary statement or other outside matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions relying on outside materials (preliminary statement, extraneous affidavits not properly before the tribunal) are not proper grounds for dissolution (see Faure v. Bradley). If outside matter raises patentability issues those should be referred to primary examiner via proper channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter‑affidavits and evidence on motion to dissolve
rubrics_metrics.description: On a motion to dissolve an interference counter‑affidavits may be filed at the time named for the hearing and without notice; affidavits filed without leave will not be noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts/trial tribunals may permit counter‑affidavits; if adverse party is surprised a continuance may be granted. Affidavits must comply with rules governing evidence submission; unauthorized filings will be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: If both parties do not claim same subject‑matter, interference dissolved
rubrics_metrics.description: That if both parties do not claim the same subject‑matter the interference will be dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference requires a genuine conflict in claimed subject matter; divergence in claims that shows no overlapping subject matter leads to dissolution (cases: Sawyer v. Edison; Dod v. Cobb). Examiner examines claim scope to determine this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operativeness/usefulness as ground for dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two machines in interference are different, and only one is operative, the difference will be treated as essential and dissolution may be ordered; if only one of the inventions is useful and operative a dissolution will be ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one claimed device is inoperative or not useful, that can be ground for dissolving the interference (see Bradford v. Imlay; Fuller v. Brush). Examiners will consider operability/usefulness evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventorship and dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: If the contestants appear to be joint inventors dissolution will be ordered; where patentees in a joint conflicting patent were not joint inventors the interference will be dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showings of joint inventorship (or lack thereof) affect interference status. Allegations that parties are joint inventors can result in dissolution or other judgment adjustments (see Taylor v. Martin; Walton v. Dennis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation that adverse party is not original inventor requires conclusive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: If a motion to dissolve is made on the ground that the adverse party is not an original inventor, the allegation must be conclusively proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenging inventorship is a heavy burden; mere assertion insufficient. Courts/case law require conclusive proof before dissolution on this ground (see Hockhausen v. Weston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two motions on same ground not permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Two motions to dissolve cannot be entertained on the same ground; one motion with appeal or rehearing is allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedy by one full motion and then appeal; repetitive motions on identical grounds are barred (see Banks v. Snediker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of disclaimer by later applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: If the later applicant disclaims the invention the interference will be dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A later applicant may file a disclaimer of the contested matter (see Laverty v. Flagg). The disclaimer mechanism (see §608b) requires written signed disclaimer with two witnesses and accompanying amendment removing contested matter from claims; judgment is rendered against disclaimer and remaining application proceeds ex parte.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements and effect of a disclaimer during interference (§608b)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may file in the Patent Office a disclaimer in writing over his own signature and attested by two witnesses, averring that he does not claim to be the inventor of the particular matter in issue; the disclaimer must be accompanied by an amendment to the specification removing the contested matter from his claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclaimer must be timely (before the date fixed for preliminary statement presentation) and accompanied by amendment. The disclaimer is different from a patentee's disclaimer to amend an issued patent. If assignment exists, assignee's written consent is required. On disclaimer judgment will be rendered against him and his remaining application proceeds ex parte.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawing uncontested matter to new application (§609)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application covers several complete inventions and an interference has been declared as to less than all, the applicant may file an amendment withdrawing uncontested matters to make them subject of a new application while interference proceeds on disputed matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New application is examined ex parte and cannot contain claims that include anything still claimed in original application, though description of devices may be included as necessary for intelligibility. If the withdrawn matter later forms the basis for division, rules regarding divisionals and disclaimers apply (see Ex parte Wheeler; Clarke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of interference when non‑priority issues discovered (§606)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the examiner of interferences or the examiners‑in‑chief upon appeal discover any fact not bearing on the question of priority, but showing that no conflict actually exists between the inventions, or that the invention is not patentable to either party, or that the interference was irregularly declared, it is their duty to suggest it to the Commissioner so that he may suspend the interference and remand the case to the primary examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension is used to permit primary examiner to consider non‑priority issues (patentability, irregularity, absence of conflict). After primary examiner decision, interference may be dissolved or reinstated. Suspension may also be ordered to add new parties or when new references are found. Judgment otherwise ready will not be suspended to decide collateral questions not affecting defeated party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference examiner cannot determine patentability or consider certain affidavit evidence on public use
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner of interferences has no jurisdiction over questions of patentability, and cannot consider affidavits as to public use and reject an application or dissolve an interference on that ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues of patentability and public use should be referred to primary examiner; examiner of interferences may, however, be ordered to investigate public use or set times for taking evidence on public use by Commissioner order (see Hedges v. Daniels; Ex parte Finch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions do not stay proceedings unless specifically sought
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion does not necessarily operate as a stay of the proceedings; to effect a stay a special application must be made to the tribunal and granted on sufficient grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties want proceedings suspended while a motion is decided they must petition for a stay; ordinary motions leave interference timeline intact unless tribunal orders suspension (see DuBois v. McCloughry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery/receipt of newly discovered evidence may be permitted during hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: A hearing on an interference will be opened to let in newly discovered evidence as to the novelty of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may admit newly discovered evidence at hearing; where patentability issues first appear on hearing they may be noted and referred to primary examiner for further action. The Commissioner must take notice of objections to patentability when brought to his attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of interference judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment in an interference, if not appealed from, is conclusive on the parties to the interference as far as the action of the Patent Office is concerned; it is equivalent to a rejection of the defeated applications and a patent is awarded to the victorious applicant alone. If neither party proves priority, judgment is rendered against both to enable appeals; if an applicant establishes priority against an issued patent, an additional patent may be issued to him but the existing patent is not vacated by the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference decisions finalize Patent Office action between those parties and bar subsequent Office interferences over same invention between same parties. The wrongful issue of a patent during interference does not permit issuing another to rival absent proof of priority. Defeated party retains equity remedy (bill in equity) where Office remedies exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals in interference cases are limited to priority issues and follow defined channels
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal from an interference decision lies only on some question involved in the issue of priority and is taken in the first instance to the examiners‑in‑chief and from their adverse judgment to the Commissioner in person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals address priority questions; relation between examiners and Commissioner akin to one court to another. On appeal Commissioner should consider law and evidence; concurrent fact findings by examiners carry weight. No further appeal lies from Commissioner; defeated party may pursue equity remedies in courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority rules as between foreign patents/applicants and U.S. inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention made in the United States has priority over a foreign invention unless the foreign invention was used, published, or patented in the U.S. before the domestic invention. As between two foreign inventors who are applicants in the U.S., the first applicant in the U.S. has priority if he is an original inventor; where one has a foreign patent, the foreign patentee may have superior right in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one applicant has an earlier foreign patent, that may afford superior right; when both have foreign patents the earliest patentee has superior right. Foreign patentees stand like other applicants until contest begins and must then prove priority. Earliest introducer into U.S. may prevail when no foreign patent exists (cases cited: Lauder v. Crowell; Launder v. Crowell).
